newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British core inflation at two-year low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British core inflation at two-year low.

text.p: Britain's embattled ruling Conservatives have come within a whisker of their aim of reducing core inflation to 2.5 percent or lower by the end of the current parliament, official data published on Thursday showed.
The core inflation rate, which excludes home loans dipped to an annual 2.7 percent in March, its lowest level for two years.
The monthly rise was 0.3 percent taking the annual growth figure down from 2.9 percent in February, according to official figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Britain's finance Minister Kenneth Clarke immediately seized on the data as proof that his Conservative party had made the country one of the strongest economies in Europe.
"Britain's economy is booming while inflation stays well under control," he said.
The opposition Labour Party, widely expected to sweep to power at the May 1 election, "could wreck the best economic prospects for a generation," he said.

The Conservatives have tried to make "Britain is booming" the centrepiece of their election campaign but have so far failed to win credit from voters. Their opinion poll ratings remain low despite a raft of encouraging economic news.
"The Conservatives have slipped on too many banana skins and that has undermined their credibility," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said.
"It may be that the economic recovery is been viewed as more down to luck than judgement," he said.
The latest batch of inflation data were well received by financial markets with a rise in the pound and government bonds although shares were unimpressed.
But there are nagging concerns that inflationary pressures are already in the pipeline and will translate into inflation later this year.

Most of the fall in March inflation was because of unusually sharp falls in food prices with overall food prices dipping by 1.6 percent, the biggest fall since April 1960. Analysts warn there is no guarantee that this will be repeated.
Moreover, the data showed retailers felt able to slap higher prices on their new ranges of goods, hinting that British consumers are now much less bargain-hungry.
"We'll see inflation trough in the next two or three months," said Stewart Robinson, economist at Lombard Street Research. "After that, it will be on quite a firmly rising trend."
Analysts say that whichever party wins the election will have no choice but to raise Britain's six percent interest rates to rein in consumer demand.
They say the only question now is whether that rise needs to be 1/4 or 1/2 point.
"We suspect that the data are consitent with a modest 25 basis point rise in rates after the election," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins.
